title: Kyoto School
keyWorks: Nishida Kitarō, An Inquiry into the Good (1911)
Nishida Kitarō, From the Acting to the Seeing (1927)
Kuki Shūzō, The Structure of Iki (1930)
summary: The Kyoto School is a circle of twentieth-century Japanese philosophers that formed around Kyoto University. Nishida Kitarō, Tanabe Hajime, Nishitani Keiji and Kuki Shūzō brought European philosophy together with the experience of Zen Buddhism and Japanese culture. Their central theme is "nothingness," understood not as an empty absence or a cause for despair, but as an open space in which everything can be itself.
onEmotions: For Nishida Kitarō, the starting point is not the thought "I feel" but "pure experience," experience before it splits into subject and object: first there is the feeling itself, and only afterwards an "I" to whom it belongs. Every experience takes place in some "place" (basho in Japanese), and the deepest place is "absolute nothingness": not a void, but an openness that holds everything and stands against nothing. Nishitani Keiji showed that the experience of meaninglessness, nihilism, is not a dead end but a crack you can pass through, further on, to śūnyatā (Buddhist emptiness), where every thing and every feeling regains its own place and freedom. In The Structure of Iki, Kuki Shūzō described an aesthetic dignity: feeling deeply yet lightly, with pride and the ability to let go.

anxiety.text: Along a canal in Kyoto runs the Philosopher's Path, where Nishida Kitarō walked every day. When the future feels shaky and everything inside tightens, his walking kind of thought can turn out to be surprisingly practical. He would point out that in anxiety we usually stand "outside": I'm here, and the threat is over there, ahead. But in what he called "pure experience," experience before the split into "I" and "world," anxiety is simply what is happening now: a tightness in the chest, racing thoughts. The future we fear exists only as an image in the present. Nishida spoke of the "eternal now": every moment holds both past and future. Hence a simple conclusion: you don't have to settle tomorrow today. It's enough to stay where the anxiety actually lives, in this moment, and see that the moment is wider.
anxiety.practice: Walk for a few minutes, around the room or down the street, the way Nishida walked his path: with no goal. With each step note: "here is a step," "here is a thought about tomorrow," "here is the wind." Let the anxiety walk beside you, not ahead.

fear.text: Picture the world as a field where everything stands against you like a rival. For Nishitani Keiji, that is the ordinary view from inside fear, an ancient and honest answer to threat. He observed that ordinary consciousness structures the whole world as opposition: I am the subject, and everything else is objects that face me and may threaten me. This is not a mistake but one level of experience, which he called the "field of consciousness." Beneath it lies a deeper field, śūnyatā, Buddhist emptiness, where things do not stand against us but share one open space with us. This doesn't cancel danger or demand fearlessness from you. Rather, fear is not the whole world but one event within it. Notice the spaciousness in which the fear arose, and you find something to stand on: you are more than the point it is aimed at.
fear.practice: Sit down and slowly widen your attention in circles: your breath, the chair beneath you, the walls of the room, the sounds of the street, the sky above the house. The fear stays at the center, but more and more room opens around it, the very field Nishitani wrote about.

sadness.text: Where does philosophy begin? The Greeks answered: with wonder. A Japanese philosopher answered differently, and the sadness you're carrying now would not have struck him as something to hurry away. Nishida Kitarō, who lived through the deaths of several of his children, wrote that philosophy begins not with wonder but with "the deep sorrow of life." For him sorrow is not a malfunction but one of the most genuine ways in which life becomes aware of itself. In sadness we feel the fragility and preciousness of what we have, and that knowledge is not false. The Japanese culture from which the Kyoto School grew has the expression mono no aware, a poignant feeling for things and their touching transience. So you don't have to fix sadness; you can let it be depth: it sharpens your sight and makes your heart more attentive to the world.
sadness.practice: Look out of the window at something passing: a cloud, light on a wall, a leaf on a branch. Let your sadness look along with you. That is mono no aware: not driving the feeling away, but letting it make your seeing finer.

quote.text: The motive of philosophy must be not "wonder" but the deep sorrow of life.
quote.author: Nishida Kitarō

grief.text: Tanabe Hajime's wife died in 1951, while he lived in seclusion below the volcano Asama. He didn't rush the grief, which needs time; he thought alongside it. One of the Kyoto School's leading philosophers, he came after her death to the idea of an "existential communion" between the living and the dead: the one we love goes on acting in us, in our decisions, in the way we now love others. This is not a consolation of the "it's all in the past" kind but a description of a real bond. Nishida Kitarō, who himself lost several children, believed such pain shouldn't be overcome by reasoning: in it life becomes aware of itself most deeply. So you can give grief its place without demanding that you "let go" soon. The bond with the one who is gone doesn't break; it changes form.
grief.practice: Do one small thing today the way the person you lost would have done it: in their manner, with their kind of care. Tanabe would call it communion: they go on acting through your hands.

loneliness.text: The essay "I and Thou" holds a near-paradox: the deeper I go into myself, the closer I come to the other. When you feel cut off from everyone, that sounds strange, yet the essay speaks to such hours. Nishida wrote there that the "I" becomes itself only through meeting a "Thou," an absolutely other who cannot be dissolved into oneself. In the very depth of one's own "I" we find not a locked room but an openness toward the other. Nishitani developed the same idea: in the field of emptiness nothing exists separately; each is held up by all the others. Then loneliness is the pain of a connection with no way out for now, not proof that you are alone in the universe. Even now you are held by the people who grew the bread, built the house, wrote the words you are reading.
loneliness.practice: Send one person a short "you came to mind today," with no explanation and no expectation of a reply. For Nishida, the "I" comes alive in the very act of addressing a "Thou," not in the answer.

anger.text: The geisha of old Edo whom Kuki Shūzō wrote about carried themselves with a proud straightness: no fawning, no breaking. That bearing knows something about anger, which often guards something valuable: a boundary, dignity, justice. In The Structure of Iki, Kuki described ikiji, an inner resilience, a pride of spirit that refuses to bend. This is close to the healthy core of anger. But true iki, for Kuki, always joins resilience with akirame, detachment, the ability not to cling. Pride without clinging becomes free: you keep your back straight, but you don't have to carry the anger all your life. Nishida would add: in its first instant, anger is simply the heat of immediate experience, before the story of "it's his fault." In that instant you have a choice about how to hold that heat.
anger.practice: Stand up and straighten your back: that is ikiji, a proud bearing. Then, without slumping, let your shoulders drop and unclench your fists: that is akirame. Stand like this for a minute: upright, clinging to nothing.

shame.text: Nishitani liked an image from Zen: the eye cannot see itself. In shame it feels as if you see right through yourself, and you want to hide from every pair of eyes. He himself described the ordinary "I" as a consciousness that constantly turns itself into an object: looking at itself from outside, judging, comparing. In shame this gaze becomes unbearably sharp: you see yourself only as a "bad thing" in others' eyes. But for Nishitani a person runs deeper than any picture of themselves. In the field of emptiness a person is not an object but an openness in which actions, judgments and shame itself arise. This doesn't mean shame can't point to something important. But it speaks about an action or an image, not about your essence, which no judgment can capture.
shame.practice: Close your eyes and remember: fire does not burn itself, the eye does not see itself. Say silently: "What my shame sees is not yet the one who sees." For half a minute, be the one looking rather than the picture.

guilt.text: What does a philosopher do when he realizes his thinking failed to prevent catastrophe? In 1945 Tanabe Hajime did not justify himself. Guilt is a sign that you, too, care. At the end of the war, he wrote Philosophy as Metanoetics, from the Greek metanoia, repentance, a change of mind. He admitted that his own thinking had proven powerless in the face of catastrophe, and he saw in that admission not an end but a beginning: when we stop justifying ourselves and defending our image, a possibility of renewal opens up that a person cannot produce by their own strength alone. For Tanabe, repentance is not self-flagellation but a turning: strength comes when we acknowledge the limit of our strength. So guilt can become not a verdict but a door.
guilt.practice: Say aloud one honest sentence about what happened, with no excuses and no self-flagellation. Tanabe called this zange, repentance: not a trial of yourself but a turning. Then sketch one small action that could set something right.

envy.text: "Learn of the pine from the pine, of the bamboo from the bamboo": Nishitani loved these words of Bashō. Envy does the opposite: it measures you by someone else until they seem to have what you're incomplete without, and that stings. It lives in a world of comparisons, where everything is measured on a single scale: more or less, better or worse. Nishitani called this way of seeing the "field of consciousness," where things are mere objects to compare. In the deeper "field of emptiness," each thing, as he put it, is "at home" in its incomparable way of being. The pine is not inferior to the bamboo; it is simply a pine. Envy points to a desire worth hearing, but it is mistaken in one thing: that your life is a failed copy of someone else's. It is not a copy; it is one of a kind.
envy.practice: Find two different objects near you, say a cup and a spoon, and look at each as if it were "at home": the spoon loses nothing to the cup. Then ask: what desire of my own stands behind the envy?

emptiness.text: Nishitani Keiji admitted that in his youth nihilism was not a topic for him but the air he breathed. So he wouldn't argue with the feeling that everything has lost its color. He distinguished two kinds of "emptiness." The first is nihility: the sense that meaninglessness gapes beneath everything we do. He didn't brush this experience aside; he considered it important, because it honestly destroys false supports. But for Nishitani you don't need to flee this emptiness or get stuck in it: you can pass through it to something deeper, śūnyatā, Buddhist emptiness. There "empty" means not "there is nothing" but "nothing is frozen": everything is open, connected, able to fill again. Then your emptiness is not a verdict but perhaps a cleared patch of ground where nothing has sprouted yet.
emptiness.practice: Sit for a minute as in zazen: back straight, eyes half-closed, expecting nothing and filling yourself with nothing. If the thought "I feel nothing" comes, note it and let it go like a cloud.

confusion.text: "Great doubt, great awakening," they say in Zen. When the familiar landmarks don't work and it's unclear where to go, that sounds almost like mockery, yet Nishitani took the phrase literally. In Zen Buddhism, which Nishitani Keiji drew on, the "Great Doubt" is a state in which all ready-made answers collapse and a person is left face to face with the question. Nishitani saw such doubt not as a breakdown but as a turning point: only when the old schemes stop holding can a more direct view of things open up. Nishida Kitarō would add that "pure experience" comes before all concepts: before we know what something means, we are already living inside what is happening. Confusion is an honest encounter with a reality wider than your maps. You can let it stay a little while.
confusion.practice: Take your question as a koan: repeat it to yourself slowly, on the out-breath, five or six times, without trying to answer. Let the question stand like a mountain while you simply breathe beside it.

fatigue.text: Nishitani Keiji was troubled that modern people begin to live like machines, even when they rest. If you've carried more than you can for a long time, you probably know that feeling from the inside. He saw one of the ills of modernity in the "mechanization" of the human being: we start to see ourselves as a tool that is valuable as long as it produces, achieves, copes. Such an "I" is always stretched forward toward the next task and has nowhere to return to. Nishida Kitarō called the deepest level of being a "place," that which holds all actions but is not itself an action. You are not only what you do but also the place where doing begins and where it can stop. Rest is not lost time but a return to that place.
fatigue.practice: Lie or sit down and imagine yourself not as a worker but as a place in which a body is resting, a street is sounding, breath is flowing. Two minutes: no tasks, just being that place.

boredom.text: A musician plays a piece he knows by heart and isn't bored for a second: he is wholly in the sound, with no gap between him and the music. Nishida Kitarō used this example to explain "pure experience." When time drags and everything seems long familiar, it's the other way round: a ready-made label comes between us and the world, "I've seen this already," "this won't give me anything." We experience not the thing itself but our judgment about it. For Nishida, in boredom it isn't the world that has gone empty; experience has been screened off by concepts. That's no reproach: it's how a tired mind works. But sometimes it's enough to take the label off for a minute for the most ordinary thing, the taste of water, the texture of fabric, to become an event again.
boredom.practice: Drink a glass of water as if it were the first sip of your life: the coolness, the weight of the glass, the water's path down your throat. One minute without names, only what is there.

joy.text: What if this moment had never happened? Kuki Shūzō considered that question a key to what is most precious in life. Joy is something you want simply to live, and that's right; the question will only make it brighter. Nishida Kitarō might say that joy is close to what he called "pure experience": in moments of real joy the gap between "me" and what I rejoice in disappears, and there is simply a shining event. In The Problem of Contingency, Kuki reflected that much in life comes not out of necessity but as an encounter, as something that might not have happened. Joy is often just that: the gift of a coincidence. So it doesn't need to be held onto or justified. It's enough to notice that it's here and let it be fully present for as long as it lasts.
joy.practice: Say to yourself ichigo ichie, "one meeting, one time," as they say at the tea ceremony. Then name in one sentence what is making you glad right now and why it will never happen in exactly this way again.

love.text: Between two people, Kuki Shūzō wrote, a gap must remain, or the attraction dies. A strange thought when you love and want to be closer, but what stands behind it is tenderness, not calculation. In the essay "I and Thou," Nishida Kitarō wrote that a genuine relationship with another arises when I recognize in them an absolute other who cannot be appropriated, and that this is exactly how I myself become who I am. In The Structure of Iki, Kuki himself described bitai, a sensual allure that stays alive as long as some distance remains between two people, as long as the other isn't swallowed up. For Kuki, graceful love combines attraction with pride and a lightness in letting go. Tenderness, then, requires neither merging nor possession: it breathes in the space between you and the other. That space is not coldness but the place where love stays free.
love.practice: Picture someone you love at a moment when they can't see you: walking down a street, lost in their own thoughts. Spend a minute feeling tenderness toward that separate life of theirs, closed to you, toward the "Thou" Nishida called absolutely other.

quote.text: Iki is a sensual allure (coquetry) that is refined (resignation) and full of tension (pride of spirit).
quote.author: Kuki Shūzō

gratitude.text: People in Japan say okagesama de, "thanks to your shade," even when no one in particular has helped. In this phrase gratitude is addressed to the whole world, which suddenly feels generous. Nishitani Keiji described the field of emptiness as one in which each thing is held up by all the others: nothing exists on its own; everything is a knot of countless connections. Okagesama de is a quiet acknowledgment that we are alive thanks to unseen support. Gratitude here is not politeness or duty but an accurate perception of reality: you really are held by many hands. And that knowledge can be calming: you don't have to hold everything up alone. Gratitude simply lets you see the web you are already in.
gratitude.practice: Before your next meal or cup of tea, put your palms together for a second and say itadakimasu, "I humbly receive." Silently recall at least three people whose hands are in this food.

hope.text: In spring the cherry trees blossom in Kyoto, and everyone knows the petals will fall within a week and bloom again next year. The Kyoto philosophers saw in such rhythms not sorrow but openness, and hope, which keeps us on the road, lives right there. For Nishida Kitarō, the future does not lie somewhere far ahead: it is born inside the "eternal now," in every moment where past and future meet. And the emptiness Nishitani Keiji wrote about means that nothing is frozen forever, neither circumstances nor you yourself. If the world were a set of unchanging things, there would be nothing to hope for. But it is open. Hope, then, is not a fantasy but a sensitivity to that openness. It doesn't need to know how everything will end; it's enough to see that nothing has ended yet.
hope.practice: Look out of the window and find something that is changing right now: a cloud, a shadow, a branch, people at a bus stop. Watch for a minute how nothing stays put: that is the openness hope leans on.

nostalgia.text: Kuki Shūzō spent eight years in Europe, talked with Bergson, listened to Heidegger, and then wrote his major book about the taste of old Edo, which was already vanishing. He knew how the past glows when it can't be brought back. In The Structure of Iki he described akirame, detachment, a knowledge of the impermanence of things that makes feeling not heavier but more graceful. Detachment here is not cold: it is the ability to love without demanding that the beloved stay forever. Nishida Kitarō would add that the past has not simply vanished: it goes on living in the "eternal now," in who you have become. Nostalgia, then, is the past breathing in you, not a lost paradise.
nostalgia.practice: Repeat one gesture from that time: brew tea the way you did then, hum that tune, tie a scarf the old way. Notice that the past lives not only in memory but in the body, in the "eternal now."

craving.text: Zen has an image: the wave is not separate from the ocean, yet the ocean doesn't turn into the wave. When "I want it right now" rolls in, that's worth remembering, and there's nothing shameful in the craving itself. Drawing on Buddhism, Nishitani Keiji described the ordinary "I" as a center that keeps reaching for things, trying to fill a sense of lack beneath itself. Craving is one of the most vivid forms of this movement. Nishida Kitarō would suggest looking at it as "pure experience": before the story "I need this" there are just sensations, heat, tension, an image, an impulse. If you watch them without merging with them, you can see that the craving is a wave: it rises, peaks and falls. You are not the wave but the place it passes through. The place holds the wave and stays whole.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, count your out-breaths from one to ten, as in zazen, and with each one note where the wave is in your body and how strong it is. Lost count? Start again at one. Watch the wave rise and fall.

addiction.text: Japanese Buddhism distinguishes jiriki, "self-power," from tariki, "other power," help you can't order yourself to produce. For someone whom addiction has pulled into a loop around a single point, this distinction is neither abstract nor a moral reproach. In Philosophy as Metanoetics, Tanabe Hajime described the experience of those who have made their way out of such a loop: the moment a person honestly admits they can't manage on their own strength alone, by willpower alone. For Tanabe this admission is not defeat but a turning: where the proud "I'll do it myself" ends, "other power" opens up, support that comes from outside, from other people and from life itself. This resonates with the experience of people in mutual-help groups. Admitting your powerlessness doesn't mean giving up. It means no longer fighting alone.
addiction.practice: Say aloud the name of one person or mutual-help group with whom you could talk honestly about your loop. Tanabe would say that this is how "other power" already begins to act. You don't have to call right now.

hangover.text: "Every day is a good day," the Zen master Yunmen answered when asked about the future. On a hard morning after, that sounds almost like mockery: your body aches, and on top of that come anxiety, shame, scraps of last night. All of this happens, and scolding yourself on top of it only adds pain to pain. Nishida Kitarō spoke of the "eternal now": every moment is a new beginning in which the past is present but doesn't determine everything. Yesterday has already happened; today is a different place. Tanabe Hajime distinguished self-flagellation from repentance: the first keeps us circling in guilt, the second turns us toward renewal. You don't have to reconstruct last night minute by minute or pass sentence on yourself. It's enough to look after your body and notice that this morning, too, can be lived gently.
hangover.practice: Wash your face with cool water and stand for a couple of minutes by an open window. On the in-breath, silently: "a new morning"; on the out-breath: "yesterday is over." Nothing more is needed for now.

euphoria.text: In Japanese summers they set off hanabi, "fire flowers," and no one tries to hold them in the sky. The flash of feeling that anything is possible is like them. Nishida Kitarō would probably recognize in it features of "pure experience": the gap between "I" and the world disappears and everything flows as one stream. It's a valuable experience, and there's no need to be suspicious of it. Kuki Shūzō would add only one thing: the lightness he called akirame, detachment, the ability to enjoy without grasping. Euphoria is by nature fleeting, like fireworks on a summer night, and part of its beauty lies in that fleetingness. You can live the high fully and still not demand that it last forever; then its ending will be not a fall but the natural ebb of a wave.
euphoria.practice: Live the high through your body: walk a little, stretch, feel where in your body this light is. Then tell yourself what people say of hanabi: "beautiful, and let it burn out on its own." Big decisions can wait until tomorrow.

crash.text: For reality, Nishida Kitarō found a formula that sounds like an oxymoron: "absolutely contradictory self-identity." When a moment ago everything was bright and now it's grey and empty, the formula suddenly becomes very concrete. It means that opposites don't cancel each other out but make up one movement. The rise and the fall are not enemies but two phases of one wave, like breathing in and breathing out. So the current low doesn't disprove your recent joy, nor does it prove that "it'll be like this forever now." It is simply the other side of the same movement. Nishitani Keiji would remind you that in the field of emptiness nothing freezes for good, including this greyness. You can wait it out the way you wait out low tide, knowing the sea hasn't gone anywhere.
crash.practice: Take ten slow breaths in and out, noting: the in-breath is the rise, the out-breath is the fall, and both are one breath. For today, allow yourself the bare minimum of demands.

panic.text: In Zen monasteries they teach: when you don't know what to do, feel your feet. When your heart pounds, your breathing falters and something irreversible seems about to happen, that's advice, not a metaphor. It really is terrifying, and you don't need to "understand" anything right now. You can simply remind yourself that a wave like this usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Nishida Kitarō stressed that "pure experience" is first of all what is felt right now, before any interpretation. In panic the mind races toward frightening stories about the future; what steadies you is the immediate: your feet, the surface under your palms, the objects around you. The Kyoto School would add: the place the wave passes through is bigger than the wave. The task is not to stop it but to wait it out, holding on to the present.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and feel the heel, the arch, the toes, as in kinhin, slow Zen walking. Take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath, and name aloud three things you can see.

dread.text: The Japanese title of Nishitani Keiji's major book is What Is Religion?, but underneath it lies another question, one that may be sounding in you now: "what's the point of it all?" It comes when familiar meanings give way and an abyss opens underfoot. Nishitani called this experience "nihility," a nothingness that gapes beneath everything that exists, and he didn't consider it a weakness. On the contrary: for Nishitani this question is the beginning of real depth, because in it a person stops living on autopilot. But the abyss is not the last word. If you pass through it, śūnyatā, emptiness, opens up: the same "nothing," now seen not as a void but as a spaciousness in which everything exists freely and regains its meaning. Your dread, then, is not an answer but a question, and that question goes on.
dread.practice: In the evening, step outside or go to a window and look at the sky for a minute or two. Don't look for an answer to "why": just stay in the spaciousness Nishitani called emptiness, not a void but an open place.

fomo.text: Where are you right now? Nishida Kitarō built a whole philosophy of "place," basho, on that simple question. The fear of missing out answers it painfully: real life is happening somewhere out there, to other people, and you are in the wrong place. For him every experience and every "I" is always already in some place, and that place is no worse and no better than another: it is simply where reality unfolds for you. Nishitani Keiji added that in the field of emptiness every thing is "at home," in its own unique way of being. So you can't be in "the wrong place": where you are, a full piece of the world is happening, and the feed of other people's events is only images within your own place. The only thing you can truly miss is what is happening here.
fomo.practice: Put your phone face down and step out for five minutes: onto a balcony, into the yard, to a window. Find three things happening only here: a sound, a light, a smell. That is your basho.

sleepless.text: In Zen monasteries night is not empty time: monks sometimes sit until dawn, simply listening to the dark. But when you can't sleep and at three in the morning everything seems bigger and more hopeless, the dark feels quite different. Nishida Kitarō called the deepest level of reality "absolute nothingness," and that is not a frightening void but a boundless place that holds everything and stands against nothing. Night is a little like it: the forms of the day dissolve, and a dark open space remains. Thoughts sound loud in it because they have nothing to compete with. You don't have to fight them or try to solve them: they are only waves in a dark expanse, not a verdict. Conclusions reached at night are rarely accurate; they can wait until morning, and meanwhile you can simply lie in a silence that asks nothing of you.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, listen to the dark the way monks do at a night sitting: the farthest sound, then a nearer one, then your own breathing. To each intrusive thought, a short "in the morning."

betrayal.text: The other person, for Nishida Kitarō, is a "Thou," absolutely other: they can never be fully understood from the inside or guaranteed. When trust collapses, and with it a world in which this person was a support, the thought sounds bitter, and yet there is comfort in it. So trust is always both a gift and a risk. Betrayal doesn't mean you were naive to trust: without that risk there's no closeness at all. Kuki Shūzō would suggest a combination of ikiji, a pride of spirit that won't let itself be trampled, and akirame, a detachment that over time helps you stop carrying the person who hurt you. So you can acknowledge the wound and keep your dignity, without letting the pain become your new essence.
betrayal.practice: Write on a slip of paper: "I was hurt. That's true. And I remain someone capable of trust." Read it aloud with your back straight, with ikiji, pride of spirit, and notice which part of the sentence sounds strongest.

jealousy.text: Kuki Shūzō noticed something strange: attraction lives only while there is distance between two people. Yet when the fear of losing someone you love mixes with pain and anger, you want to shrink that distance to nothing. In The Structure of Iki, he described bitai, an allure that stays alive only as long as the other remains other: free, not appropriated. For Kuki, genuine sensuality rests on the tension of distance, and trying to possess a person completely kills it. This isn't a reproach: jealousy is natural, and it shows how precious the person is to you. But Kuki's idea suggests that love is by its nature not property and can't be secured by control. You can acknowledge your fear and at the same time see that the other's freedom is not a threat to love but the condition that makes love possible at all.
jealousy.practice: Imagine the person you love as free: going about their day, laughing with someone, thinking their own thoughts. Breathe for a minute, letting the picture simply be, and notice where in your body the fear tightens and where it lets go.

resentment.text: There's a Zen story: two monks carry a woman across a stream, and hours later, when the younger is still indignant, the elder says: "I set her down on the bank; you're still carrying her." An old grievance is like that burden: it reminds you of an injustice, and setting it down feels like betraying yourself. Kuki Shūzō valued ikiji, pride of spirit, a refusal to be humiliated. But he also showed that in a graceful character it is joined with akirame, a detachment grounded in the Buddhist knowledge of impermanence. Akirame is not forgiveness out of obligation, nor agreement with what happened. It is a loosening of the grip: the grievance stops being the place where you live. Nishida Kitarō would add: you are a "place" that holds many experiences, not one of them. Then the grievance can remain a memory without defining the whole of you.
resentment.practice: Hold a stone or any heavy object in your hand for a minute, feeling its weight, then slowly set it down. Say to yourself: "Let it lie on the bank."

heartbreak.text: What is left of love once it has ended? The Kyoto philosophers answered unexpectedly: almost everything. A life that was shared has suddenly come apart, and it hurts almost physically; there's no need to hurry to "go through it properly." In The Structure of Iki, Kuki Shūzō described akirame, a detachment that, in his words, grows out of experience, including the experience of disappointment in love: a person learns that everything is impermanent, and that makes their feelings not cold but refined. Nishida Kitarō would remind you that what you have lived through does not vanish; it becomes part of the "place" that you are. The love that was there was real, even if it ended. The pain of parting, then, is not proof that it was all a mistake but the trace of a depth that will stay with you.
heartbreak.practice: Pour yourself some tea and drink it slowly, recalling one thing this relationship gave you that will stay with you. That is akirame in action: letting the person go without renouncing what you lived.

impostor.text: Who are you when no one is watching and there's no part to play? Zen asks this as a koan: "What was your original face before your parents were born?" The impostor feeling answers frighteningly: no one is there, and soon everyone will see. Nishitani Keiji would say this fear rests on a particular picture of the "I," as an object that can be inspected, assessed and declared fake or genuine. But for Nishitani the true "I" is not a thing with a label. It is closer to an openness in which actions, learning and mistakes take place. Nishida Kitarō called this "self-awareness": not a look at oneself from outside but a living activity. So there is no "real you" waiting to be exposed: there is you, doing the work right now. Doubt is just one thought in that process, not an expert appraisal of your essence.
impostor.practice: For five minutes, do something simple with your hands, wash a cup, water a plant, wholeheartedly, as in the Zen work practice called samu. Notice: while you are doing, there's no question of whether you're real; there is just the doing.

self_hatred.text: Picture a courtroom where the judge, the prosecutor and the accused are one and the same person. That is probably how Nishitani Keiji would describe self-hatred: a harsh judge lives inside you, one you can't get away from, but his verdict is not the truth about you. Nishitani did describe how the ordinary "I" closes in on itself: it looks at itself, judges, condemns, and this circle can grow tighter and tighter. But he also showed that beneath this circle lies the field of "emptiness," where a person can't be reduced to any judgment. There you are not a "bad object" but a living, open place in which pain, hope and the capacity for change all arise. Tanabe Hajime believed that even an honest admission of one's mistakes leads not to eternal condemnation but to renewal. The inner critic speaks loudly but sees very little.
self_hatred.practice: Say your inner critic's sentence aloud, then answer it the way you would answer a close friend who said this about themselves. Tanabe would call it a turning: not a trial but a renewal.

helplessness.text: In the autumn of 1944 Tanabe Hajime gave his last lecture course in Kyoto, on repentance and the powerlessness of philosophy. He knew helplessness from the inside: seeing what is happening and being unable to change it. During the war he came to the conclusion that his philosophy was powerless to stop anything. Out of that experience came Philosophy as Metanoetics. Tanabe didn't pretend the powerlessness wasn't there. He showed that acknowledging your limits can be freeing: we stop demanding the impossible of ourselves, and then "other power" opens up, the support of other people, of life itself, of what is greater than us. Helplessness is not proof of your worthlessness but an honest encounter with a boundary. And you don't have to stand at that boundary alone.
helplessness.practice: Take a slip of paper, write "This doesn't depend on me," and put it aside. Then find one tiny thing that does depend on you, and do it. Tanabe would say: strength comes where a limit is acknowledged.

procrastination.text: When the Zen master Zhaozhou was asked about the way, he replied: "Have you eaten? Then wash your bowl." If a task keeps getting put off, it's usually not laziness but fear, tiredness or too big a picture of the task. Nishida Kitarō described "acting intuition": we understand the world not before acting but in the acting itself; by doing we see, and by seeing we go on doing. So you can't first get fully "pulled together" and then begin: the pulling together happens inside the doing. His example of "pure experience" is a musician wholly absorbed in playing: there is no separate "I" painfully forcing itself. A task is frightening as long as you look at it from outside, as one huge object. From inside it consists of one small movement, and then the next.
procrastination.practice: Wash one cup, slowly and wholeheartedly, as Zhaozhou advised. Right after that, make the first tiny move in the task: open the file or put the thing you need on the table. Nothing more.

uprooted.text: Kuki Shūzō made the first draft of his book on the most Japanese of Japanese tastes not in Kyoto but in Paris: from far away, your own shows more clearly. Emigration, a move, losing your ground: this is the loss not of an address but of a familiar world. Kuki, who lived in Europe for about eight years, understood this well. Nishida Kitarō showed that "place," basho, is not only a point on a map. Every experience always happens somewhere, and the deepest place, "absolute nothingness," cannot be lost, because it holds all places. You haven't fallen out of the world: you are still in a place, even if it is new and unfamiliar. Roots grow slowly, but they can take hold in new soil too.
uprooted.practice: Take a short walk around your new place and find one thing that reminds you of your old home, a tree, a smell, a sound, and one thing that wasn't there. Silently greet them both.

overload.text: The Zen formula is almost cheekily simple: "When you eat, eat; when you walk, walk." The feed, the notifications and the endless stream work exactly the other way: your head is overfull and yet empty inside. Nishida Kitarō would set against it "pure experience": a whole experience with no fragmentation. A musician absorbed in playing doesn't switch every ten seconds; their attention is unified. In the information stream, on the contrary, we keep splintering into pieces and are never fully present anywhere. Nishitani Keiji saw the mechanization of life as one of the sources of the modern feeling of emptiness. The weariness of overload is not a flaw in you but a natural answer of living attention to a stream it wasn't made for. It needs a place where it can be whole again.
overload.practice: One task, one attention: for three minutes, eat, drink tea or wash your hands without switching to anything else. Phone in another room. Notice what attention feels like when it isn't being pulled anywhere.

unreality.text: The world as a stage set: things stand "over there," I watch from "here," and it's as if there were glass between us. That is how Nishitani Keiji described reality slipping away when everything is perceived merely as objects. If the world seems to be behind glass right now, or you feel as if in a dream, it can be very unsettling; it's worth describing gently, without hasty labels. For Nishitani the way to what is genuine is not more analysis but a more immediate encounter, in which a thing appears as it is. Nishida Kitarō would call such an encounter "pure experience." Unreality is not proof that the world isn't there but a sign that your connection with it is muffled right now. It can be gently restored through the simplest thing of all: sensation.
unreality.practice: Press your palms against a cool surface, a wall, a table, a windowpane, and for a minute describe aloud what you feel: smooth, cool, hard. "Pure experience" begins with the skin.

awe.text: In An Inquiry into the Good, Nishida Kitarō described a moment when "there is not yet a subject or an object." Before mountains, a starry sky or music, such moments happen on their own: we become smaller and larger at once. This is "pure experience" in almost pure form: the usual division into me and the world disappears, and only the radiance of what is happening remains. For him this is not an illusion but a more primary reality: first there is experience, and only then an "I" who has it. Nishitani Keiji would call it drawing near to the field of emptiness, an open expanse in which each thing appears in all its uniqueness. Awe doesn't need to be explained or held onto. It reminds you: you are part of something infinitely spacious.
awe.practice: Go out under the sky, onto a balcony, into the yard, and for a minute look at the farthest thing you can see: a cloud, a star, a treetop. Don't take a photo or search for words.

quote.text: It is not that experience exists because there is an individual, but that an individual exists because there is experience.
quote.author: Nishida Kitarō
quote.source: An Inquiry into the Good (1911), preface

relief.text: Dōgen, the thirteenth-century Zen teacher, spoke of "dropping off body and mind," a moment when everything you were holding on to suddenly lets go. Relief is a small relative of that moment: the exhale after long tension, which you can simply live. The Kyoto School would add that there is something very honest in relief: we suddenly feel how much strength it took to hold on. Nishida Kitarō spoke of a "place" that holds all experiences; in relief we feel that place for a moment, spacious and uncluttered. Kuki Shūzō valued lightness, the ability to let go and not cling to what has passed; relief is the most natural expression of that lightness. There's no need to go looking for the next worry right away or to fear that the good won't last. You can let your body and mind feel the space that has opened up.
relief.practice: On an in-breath, lift your shoulders to your ears, and on the out-breath let them drop. Repeat three times, as if shedding "body and mind" as Dōgen said, then for half a minute stay where the relief is strongest.

calm.text: The sky doesn't get in the way of clouds and doesn't cling to them. Nishida Kitarō, who sat in Zen meditation for years, described "absolute nothingness" this way: the deepest place, which holds everything, joy and anxiety alike, yet itself stays unperturbed. The calm you don't have to earn is like that sky: it doesn't depend on whether everything has been sorted out. Nishitani Keiji said that in the field of emptiness every thing is "at home." Calm may be exactly that feeling of being at home, in your own present moment. It is not an absence of life but its quiet fullness. You can simply enjoy it.
calm.practice: For a minute, do nothing: don't meditate "properly," don't try to enjoy it. Just sit like a sky with clouds drifting across it, letting thoughts pass without snagging on anything.

inspiration.text: "From the created to the creating": that is how Nishida Kitarō described the movement of history, in which each of us is at once a result of the past and the beginning of something new. Inspiration is the moment you feel this in your skin, as if something wants to be born through you, and the world briefly becomes a workshop. In this sense inspiration is not a random spark but a moment when you feel especially clearly that you are a creative point in the world. His "acting intuition," the unity of seeing and doing, describes well how in inspiration thought and hand seem to move at the same time. So inspiration doesn't need to be controlled or rationed. Better simply to start doing while the wave is carrying you, and think about the result later.
inspiration.practice: Without thinking it over, write down or sketch what has come to you, right now: messily, with a hand that sees as it works. That is "acting intuition." You can polish it later.

schadenfreude.text: Imagine a ladder on which everyone stands: someone next to you slips, and you seem to be one rung higher. That, for Nishitani Keiji, is how the ordinary "I" sees the world, a center that measures everything relative to itself. Schadenfreude, which frightens us ourselves, is born on this imaginary ladder and says little about who you are. This is the standpoint of the "field of consciousness," where I and the other are separate objects competing for a place. But Nishitani also spoke of a deeper "field of emptiness," where things don't stand against one another but hold each other up. Schadenfreude is a flash of comparison, not your essence. Once you notice it, you don't need to fight it; you can ask what worry about your own place it is responding to.
schadenfreude.practice: Silently wish the person who slipped one simple thing: "May it work out for you." You don't have to mean it; just notice what happens in your body as you step down the ladder.

contempt.text: Where is the contemptuous gaze looking from? It's a very Kyoto question: what matters is not only what you see but from which "place." Contempt often holds some truth: something really does seem petty or unworthy to you. Nishida Kitarō said that every experience takes place in some "place" (basho in Japanese). Contempt is a place above: I stand on a height, the other is below, and between us there's a solid wall. In "absolute nothingness," Nishida's deepest place, there is no such height: both you and the one you despise arise in the same openness. At the same time, contempt often protects you from something: disappointment, pain, an uncomfortable resemblance. It's worth questioning, not being ashamed of.
contempt.practice: Come down from the height literally: sit on the floor or a low step and look at the situation from there. Ask: "What if I didn't stand above this person?" and listen to the first answer.

disgust.text: Japanese aesthetics can find beauty in a cracked bowl or weathered wood: wabi-sabi. But there are moments when you want to turn away, draw back, close up: disgust is a very bodily feeling, whether it's about people, situations or yourself, and it doesn't make you a bad person. Nishida Kitarō began philosophy with "pure experience," experience before we split it into "I" and "this." In such experience, disgust is at first simply a wave: tightening, nausea, recoil. Only afterwards does the mind stick a label on it: "this is vile" or "I am vile." Nishitani Keiji said that in the "field of emptiness" each thing is "at home," in its own way of being, not in the role we have assigned to it. Disgust can be endured without turning it into a final verdict on the world or on yourself.
disgust.practice: For a minute, look at something imperfect nearby, a crack in a cup, a stain on the wall, a dry leaf, in the spirit of wabi-sabi: not forcing admiration, just letting the thing be "at home." Notice where in your body there is a little more room.

revenge.text: Who does your life belong to while you're thinking about revenge? Tanabe Hajime would probably ask that. The wish for revenge is usually born of a real wound: you were treated unjustly, and your soul demands balance. Tanabe himself, who during the war saw his own convictions collapse, arrived at "metanoetics," a philosophy that begins with admitting the powerlessness of one's own "I." He wrote that true renewal comes not from "self-power" (jiriki in Japanese) but from "other power" (tariki), something that surpasses us and allows us to let go. Revenge promises release but in fact ties you more tightly to the person who hurt you, making them the center of your life. Acknowledging the pain fully and letting it be is already a step toward it no longer ruling you.
revenge.practice: On an in-breath, clench your fists as tight as you can, and on the out-breath slowly open your palms. Repeat three times. Tanabe would call it a small tariki: you don't let go by willpower; you allow your hands to let go.

anger_at_loved.text: Why do those closest to us hurt us most? The Kyoto School has an almost physical answer. Anger at a partner, a parent, a child can be very strong, and shame follows, yet anger and love don't exclude each other. Nishitani Keiji described the deep connection of things as mutual interpenetration: in the "field of emptiness" no one exists separately but through others, as if others enter into one's very being. The people closest to us penetrate us most deeply, which is why their words and actions hit where we are least protected. So your anger doesn't prove there's no love; rather, it shows how woven into your life this person is, and it may point to a boundary or a need that has long gone unnoticed. You can acknowledge the anger without dumping it on the other person or hiding it from yourself.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger has settled a little, say one sentence to the person, starting with "what matters to me is…" rather than "you always…" In a field where people interpenetrate, a request reaches deeper than a reproach.

ambivalence.text: Zen masters liked to answer the question "yes or no?" with something third. Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is exhausting, but it is an entirely human state. We usually think only one thing can be true: either I love them or I don't. In his late works Nishida Kitarō spoke of the "self-identity of absolute contradictories": the world holds together precisely because opposites coexist without merging or destroying each other. A living person, for Nishida, is not a smooth essence but a place where such tensions meet. Your mixed feelings are not a mistake to be fixed urgently by choosing a side. They are an honest reflection of a complicated relationship. You can let both feelings be, without rushing to a final decision, and see that you are wider than either of them.
ambivalence.practice: Put one palm on your chest: that is "I love." Put the other on your belly: that is "I can't stand." Breathe for a minute without removing either hand, and notice that there is room in you for both, as in Nishida's "place."

guilty_relief.text: At a Zen temple a bell is struck, and afterwards the silence rings on for a long time. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or a loved one's long illness is like that silence, and it often frightens us: how can I feel lighter when there "should" be nothing but grief? You can. Relief and love don't cancel each other out. Nishida Kitarō said that the deepest "place," "absolute nothingness," has room for everything, and one experience does not push out another. Sorrow, exhaustion from long strain and the exhale after it can all live in one heart at once. Relief often means not "I'm glad about the loss" but "something unbearably hard has ended." Allowing yourself relief is neither betrayal nor coldness. It's simply the truth about how much you were carrying, and part of how life goes on.
guilty_relief.practice: If there's a small bell, a bowl or a glass nearby, tap it lightly and listen to the sound until it fades completely. If not, just listen to the silence for a minute. There is room in it for both sorrow and the exhale.

indifference.text: In Zen poetry snow often means not cold but a silence under which the earth goes on living. Sometimes, where you're "supposed" to be moved, by important news, someone else's misfortune, even grief, there is such a silence inside, and it's frightening. But indifference rarely means you truly don't care. Nishitani Keiji wrote a great deal about nihilism, the experience in which everything suddenly loses weight and meaning. He believed this experience can't simply be muffled: you have to pass through it, and then it can open into the "field of emptiness," where things become alive and close again. Numbness is not a verdict but perhaps a pause in which the mind is saving its strength or can't yet take in what has happened. Don't force yourself to feel "the right way": an honest silence is closer to the truth than performed emotion.
indifference.practice: Sit in silence for a minute, demanding nothing of yourself, like earth under snow. If the reproach "I should be feeling something" comes, just note it and return to the sounds around you.

escape.text: In the twelfth century the poet Saigyō left his post at court and set off to wander the roads. The urge to drop everything, the job, the city, the familiar role, and be somewhere no one knows you often speaks of weariness with a life that has become too cramped. Nishida Kitarō taught that the "I" is not locked inside a role: a role is only one of the forms arising in a deeper "place," in "absolute nothingness," which nothing limits. Nishitani Keiji spoke of a thing being "at home," in its true way of being. Then the urge to escape may be a longing not so much for another city as for the freedom to be yourself without being reduced to a function. That longing deserves to be taken seriously and, without hurrying into big decisions, listened to closely: what exactly is it asking for?
escape.practice: Walk for ten minutes with no goal, like the wandering Saigyō, even if only around the block. On the way, ask yourself: "What exactly am I looking for in the place I want to run to?" Let the answer come in steps, not as a decision.

forbidden_attraction.text: For a thousand years classical Japanese poetry has written about "secret love," love for someone you "shouldn't." Such attraction can be embarrassing and unsettling, but in itself it is part of being alive and says nothing about you yet. In The Structure of Iki (1930), Kuki Shūzō described a refined feeling of attraction that rests on distance: what matters to him is neither possession nor merging, but the tension between two people who keep their freedom. He observed that when that distance disappears, the charm disappears too. Attraction to someone unavailable is often about not only the particular person but what they embody for you: another life, another version of yourself. You can look at it with curiosity, in no hurry either to condemn yourself or to decide anything.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine this attraction as a guest at a tea ceremony: you receive it and pour it tea, but you don't invite it to live in your house. Ask the guest: what other life, what version of me are you showing me?

social_anxiety.text: At a tea ceremony the guest doesn't think about how they look: all attention is in the bowl and the sound of boiling water. When fear of judgment makes simple things hard, a call, entering a room, a word, such attention seems out of reach, but it's closer than you think. Nishitani Keiji described ordinary consciousness as a "field" in which I keep looking at myself as an object: how I look, what people will think of me. In shyness this outside view becomes almost constant. Against such self-watching, Nishida Kitarō set "pure experience," absorption in what is happening, where there's no gap between the one acting and the action itself. Relief comes not from trying to be liked but when attention shifts from yourself to the task or the other person. You can notice such moments and gradually collect them.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, become a guest at a tea ceremony: pick one detail of the other person, their intonation, something in their hands, and simply observe it for half a minute. Notice what happens to your attention on yourself.

uncertainty.text: A Zen novice is given a koan with no ready answer and learns to live with it for weeks. Not knowing what comes next, with nothing to lean on, you're in a similar place, only without a teacher. Nishitani Keiji wrote about the "Great Doubt," a state in which the familiar ground is gone and every ready-made answer is in question. For him this was also an opportunity: where schemes collapse, a person meets reality directly, not through expectations. Trying to foresee everything is the "I" trying to hold the world like an object in its hands, and life is always wider than any plan. Uncertainty is not only a threat but the honest face of a life that was never known in advance. You don't need the answer right now: you can live in the part of the road already visible.
uncertainty.practice: Say aloud three things you know for certain right now: "I'm breathing," "it's evening," "the tea is still warm." Nishitani would call this the ground underfoot, which is always there, even when there's no plan.

waiting.text: A tea master spends an hour on a single bowl of tea, and no one calls it waiting. But when you're waiting for results, an answer, news, time stretches and everything seems on pause; impatience is natural here. Nishida Kitarō spoke of the "eternal now": the present moment is not an empty gap between past and future but the place where time gathers as a whole. When we wait, it's as if we leave that place and live in what hasn't arrived yet. The Zen tradition the Kyoto School drew on values simple actions: when you eat, eat; when you walk, walk. Waiting doesn't have to be lived as emptiness. While there's no answer yet, time still passes, and it holds tea, a walk, a conversation. You don't have to hurry the waiting; you can surround it with care.
waiting.practice: Make tea the way a tea master would: slowly, watching the steam, the color, the first sip. Five minutes, only tea. The waiting won't go anywhere, but it won't be the only thing.

regret.text: When a cup breaks in Japan, it is sometimes mended with gold lacquer, kintsugi, and the crack becomes its most beautiful place. Regret over what you did or didn't do, returning again and again, needn't be hidden either: it shows that you care. In the last years of the war Tanabe Hajime wrote Philosophy as Metanoetics, from the Greek metanoia, "change of mind, repentance." He acknowledged the errors of his own thinking and saw that honest acknowledgment does not destroy a person but becomes a place of renewal: through recognizing one's powerlessness comes a strength greater than the "I." Regret is not endless self-punishment but the start of a path Tanabe called "death and resurrection," giving up your former self for a new one. The past can't be changed, but how you are connected to it can.
regret.practice: Write one sentence about what you regret and circle it, like a crack traced in gold. Next to it, add what it taught you, and begin the third line with: "Now I can…"

longing.text: How can you feel someone near precisely because they are gone? For Nishida Kitarō there was no paradox in that. Their place beside you is empty, and it feels almost physical: that is how a real connection speaks. In the essay "I and Thou" (1932), he wrote that the "Thou" is absolutely other and cannot be dissolved into oneself, and yet the "I" finds the "Thou" in its own very depths: the other doesn't simply stand outside but has a part in who we have become. Longing is a person's presence in the form of their absence. Their voice, habits, jokes go on living in you, and that's why the emptiness beside you feels so sharp. You don't have to chase longing away; you can treat it as a form of faithfulness, as proof that the meeting happened.
longing.practice: Tell someone, a friend, or simply the empty room aloud, one story about this person: a joke of theirs, a habit. Let the "Thou" sound in the present tense: that is how they go on taking part in who you have become.

world_pain.text: A Buddhist image, Indra's net, has a jewel at every knot, each reflecting all the others. When grim news presses so hard that ordinary life gets difficult, you feel this is more than a metaphor: distant disaster is reflected in you, a sign of your compassion. Nishitani Keiji described reality as a web of interconnections: in the "field of emptiness" each thing is connected to all the others and reflects them. So the connection is real. But the same idea implies something else: you are not obliged to hold up the whole world alone. You are one point in this web, and your place is here, in your particular life, among the people around you. Compassion that finds a small, real action close at hand brings more relief than endlessly reading the news.
world_pain.practice: Help someone nearby today with one small thing: offer support, make a call, carry a bag. That is your knot in the net. And then give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Picture two lines that might cross, or might miss each other. When you're rejected, it feels as if not a request was turned down, but the whole of you. In The Problem of Contingency (1935), Kuki Shūzō described an encounter as an event in which two independent lines of life converge, something that might come together and might not. A refusal is an encounter that didn't align, an event between two free people, not a final assessment of your essence. Nishida Kitarō would remind you that the "I" runs deeper than any role in which it was or wasn't accepted: you are not a single image to be approved or discarded, but a living "place" where far more is happening than this one answer. You can live through the pain without agreeing with the verdict it seems to pronounce.
rejection.practice: On a slip of paper, draw two lines that pass close and never cross, and label them: "an event, not a verdict." Then name aloud three things in you that this refusal didn't touch.

abandonment.text: Tanabe Hajime has a dry term, "absolute mediation," with a warm thought behind it: nothing exists by itself; everything exists through its relationships with others. That's why the fear of being abandoned can run so deep: without the other, it seems nothing will be left to hold on to. Your need for people is not a flaw but the very fabric of life. But Nishida Kitarō would add that all relationships arise in the "place of absolute nothingness," an openness that holds every meeting and parting and doesn't vanish with any of them. In other words, connections are important and real, but the deep "place" you live in cannot leave along with someone. You can acknowledge the fear and at the same time feel the support you already have.
abandonment.practice: Imagine yourself at the center of a web: threads run from you to people, places, activities. Silently name at least three, and feel that you are not hanging on by a single thread.

unrequited.text: Can you love, receiving nothing in return, and not grow poorer? Kuki Shūzō thought so, and even found a particular grace in it. When the feeling is there but the meeting isn't, it hurts, but the love is no less real for that. In The Structure of Iki, he described romantic attraction as a tension between two people who remain separate and free. One of the elements of iki he called akirame, a Buddhist-tinged word meaning both "resignation" and "seeing clearly": the ability to accept impermanence and not cling. For Kuki this is not coldness but a particular maturity of feeling: loving without demanding that the world bend to your wish. Your love is neither a mistake nor a defeat. It showed your capacity to feel deeply. Letting go of the hope of it being returned doesn't mean devaluing the feeling itself.
unrequited.practice: Read these words to yourself slowly, twice: "I love, and that is mine; the answer is not mine." Then breathe for a minute, noticing where in your body this feeling lives, the one that asks for no answer.

humiliation.text: Can a person's dignity be taken away? Nishitani Keiji would answer: an image can be taken, but not the one who sees. When you've been humiliated, perhaps in front of others, it feels as if everything was taken, and that pain deserves acknowledgment. He would say that humiliation tries to turn you into an object, a "thing" that can be judged and discarded. But for Nishitani a person, at depth, is not an object but an openness that no one else's judgment can fully capture. Nishida Kitarō described genuine self-awareness as "seeing oneself within oneself": not through someone else's distorting mirror but from inside one's own experience. Humiliation is done to an image, not to your essence. That doesn't cancel the pain, but it helps you refuse the verdict someone tried to impose on you.
humiliation.practice: Stand up, feet shoulder-width apart, and slowly lift your head as if the crown were being drawn upward. Stand for a minute in the bearing of ikiji, a dignity that others neither grant nor take away.

body_shame.text: Nishida Kitarō said that we see things by acting: the body knows the world through the movement of hands and steps. When a glance in the mirror turns into an exam, in a world full of idealized images, that's easy to forget. He insisted that the body is not a thing we look at from outside but that through which we act in the world: through the body we see, touch, create. He called this "acting intuition," a knowing that lives in movement rather than in inspection. Body shame arises when we turn the body into a picture to be graded and forget that it is first of all our way of being alive. The body that carries you down the street, holds a cup, hugs the people you love is more than any reflection.
body_shame.practice: Make one simple movement attentively: stretch slowly, roll your wrists, walk across the room. For a minute, be a body that acts, not a picture being graded.

illness.text: We live not "in" a body but as a body: you truly understand this thought of Nishida Kitarō's when your body lets you down. Illness, pain, weakness change your whole life, and irritation, fear and sadness are natural here. Illness affects not only organs but the way you are in the world. Nishitani Keiji wrote that the experience of fragility and finitude, which we usually turn away from, can become a place where life is seen more deeply: without the usual armor it's clearer what truly matters. Illness is neither your fault nor a failure. Even within limitation there remains a "place" where you go on feeling, seeing, being in relationship. That doesn't cancel the difficulty, but it gives you something to stand on.
illness.practice: Find one sensation that is pleasant today despite the illness, warm light on your skin, a taste, someone's voice, and stay with it for a minute, as with a guest. That, too, is a "place" where you live.

pride.text: A Japanese potter stamps his mark on the bottom of a bowl: small, but clear. That is dignity without boasting, and pride in what you've done, a good and deserved feeling, can be just like that. Kuki Shūzō considered ikiji one of the pillars of human dignity: an inner resilience, a calm pride of spirit that doesn't fawn and doesn't need constant approval. In An Inquiry into the Good (1911), Nishida Kitarō wrote that the good is the realization of the personality: when a person unfolds what lies within them, they do good both for themselves and for the world. Healthy pride doesn't set you against others; it confirms that you have become a little more yourself. There's no need to hide it out of modesty or inflate it into superiority; it's enough to acknowledge it calmly.
pride.practice: Put your own mark on it: calmly, aloud, in one sentence, say what exactly you did and what quality in yourself you showed, with no "but" and no "I just got lucky." Like a potter who neither hides the mark nor blows it up.

melancholy.text: The Japanese go out to look at the autumn moon on purpose, not to cheer up but to spend time with a quiet sadness. Bright sadness is like such an evening: sorrow mingles with tenderness toward the world, and it doesn't need fixing. The Japanese culture the Kyoto School grew out of has the notion of mono no aware, the poignant charm of things that comes from sensing their transience: cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they will soon fall. Nishitani Keiji believed that emptiness, understood all the way through, is not the emptiness of loss but that in which each thing appears for the first time in all its uniqueness. Melancholy is not a malfunction but a form of clear seeing: you feel that everything passes, and so everything becomes more precious. You can simply live it, like slow music.
melancholy.practice: In the evening, find the moon in the sky, or at least a streetlight, and look at it for a minute as at tsukimi, moon-viewing: let sadness and beauty stay together for a while.
